Target / co-contaminant: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics including ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin and ofloxacin
Adsorbent / material: Critical review of carbon adsorbents: activated carbon, biochar, graphene and CNTs; comparison also discusses clay-based adsorbents
Experimental design / conditions: Critical review of FQ adsorption from water and wastewater; the paper discusses adsorption capacity and partition coefficient as comparison metrics; no new adsorption experiments are reported.
Reported result: The review identifies π–π electron donor–acceptor interactions, electrostatic interactions and pore filling as prominent reported mechanisms for FQ uptake by carbon/clay adsorbents, and states that graphene showed the highest performance within its reviewed comparison.
Model / metric: Review synthesis; partition coefficient discussed as a comparative metric
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 1, abstract; PDF p. 16, §6 Conclusions and future perspectives
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; secondary source only
Caveat / follow-up: Do not treat the review’s category ranking or compiled capacities as harmonized head-to-head results. Trace specific numerical claims to the original cited studies and retain study-condition differences.

Adsorbent / material: Activated carbon, biochar, graphene and carbon nanotube adsorbents
Experimental design / conditions: The review compiles reported experimental conditions, capacities/partition coefficients, material modifications and proposed mechanisms by adsorbent class.
Reported result: Tables 3–6 provide a structured discovery map of primary studies on activated carbon, biochar, graphene and CNTs; use them to locate the underlying original studies, not as a replacement for primary-source verification.
Model / metric: Secondary review tables; no pooled common-condition experiment
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 5, Table 3; PDF p. 8, Table 4; PDF p. 9, Table 5; PDF p. 10, Table 6
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; secondary source only
Caveat / follow-up: Every capacity and partition coefficient copied to the comparison matrix must be checked against its original primary paper, metric definition and conditions.

Adsorbent / material: Nanostructured activated pomegranate-peel biochar (nPPAB), ball-milled to <100 nm; bulk pomegranate-peel material comparator
Experimental design / conditions: Pomegranate peels washed, sun-dried 7 days, oven-dried at 100 °C for 24 h, crushed/sieved to 2 mm, then pyrolyzed at 800 °C for 2 h. Paper reports 78% mass yield after initial carbonization; subsequent activation uses 85 wt% H3PO4 (Fig. 1 describes 48 h soaking), reheating at 800 °C for 2 h, washing/drying and planetary-ball milling to <100 nm.
Reported result: Reported BET surface area: 1149.62 m²/g for nPPAB versus 8.30 m²/g for bulk pomegranate-peel comparator. The 78% yield is reported after initial heating and is not demonstrated to be the final yield after activation and milling.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 2, §2.2 and Fig. 1; PDF p. 4, §3.1.2
Evidence status: Extracted from supplied main PDF; supplementary material not supplied
Caveat / follow-up: Record chemical activation, extra heating, washing/drying and milling as process burdens. This is not pristine biochar. Final nPPAB yield after all processing is not established in the extracted main text.

Experimental design / conditions: Batch isotherm tests used initial CIP concentrations of 10–120 μg/mL (10–120 mg/L), with 10 mL solution and 0.1 g sorbent in the described tests. Table 4 reports pH 7, 420 min, 0.1 g, 25 mg/L and 298 K for the tabulated qmax comparison.
Reported result: Langmuir-fitted qmax for nPPAB is reported as 142.86 mg/g. The bulk comparator is inconsistent: Table 1 reports 5.32 mg/g while Table 4 reports 5.92 mg/g.
Value / units: 142.86 mg/g nPPAB qmax; comparator 5.32 vs 5.92 mg/g
Model / metric: Model-fitted Langmuir qmax, not an observed uptake at one equilibrium concentration
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 3, Table 1; PDF p. 8, Table 4
Caveat / follow-up: Do not reconcile the bulk comparator qmax silently. Text selects 90 min as optimum contact time; another passage says equilibrium approached at 240 min, while Table 4 reports 420 min for the tabulated qmax conditions.

Experimental design / conditions: pH experiments used pH 3, 5, 7, 9 and 12; reported nPPAB pHPZC was 2.82. Paper assigns cationic CIP below pH 6.1, zwitterionic CIP between 6.1 and 8.7, and anionic CIP above pH 8.7.
Reported result: Maximum sorption was reported at pH 7. Authors discuss hydrophobic, π–π, hydrogen-bonding and electrostatic interactions, with relative contributions depending on CIP speciation and pH.
Caveat / follow-up: These mechanisms are interpretations from pH, FTIR and thermodynamic evidence, not proof that one mechanism exclusively controls uptake. Keep pH and speciation attached to any comparison.

Experimental design / conditions: Authors tested CIP-spiked distilled water and wastewater; raw wastewater samples were filtered through Whatman cellulose filter paper. They compared batch and packed-bed reactor performance and repeated adsorption/desorption tests.
Reported result: Reported removal for CIP-spiked distilled water: 96.31% batch and 94.39% packed bed. Reported removal in filtered wastewater: 89.94% batch and 84.74% packed bed. After five adsorption cycles, removal was 81.27%, with approximately 15% of CIP reported released in the desorption test.
Model / metric: Removal percentage and reuse-cycle results; not qmax
Evidence status: Extracted from supplied main PDF; SI not supplied
Caveat / follow-up: This is a filtered, CIP-spiked wastewater test, not measurement of native antibiotics in untreated wastewater. Detailed matrix composition and supplementary analytical details were not supplied.

Adsorbent / material: Ground eucalyptus leaves, pine bark, pine needles, wood ash and mussel shell by-products (<1 mm)
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — raw/minimally processed biomass and by-product biosorbents
Experimental design / conditions: Batch tests: 0.5 g sorbent + 10 mL solution, 0.005 M CaCl2 background electrolyte, added AMX concentrations 2.5–50 μmol/L, 48 h shaking in the dark and triplicate determination. Table 1's highest measured initial concentration was 52.07 μmol/L. Materials had distinct native pH values.
Reported result: At measured C0 = 52.07 μmol/L, Table 1 reports loading/removal: pine needles 1001.32 μmol/kg / 100%; wood ash 934.21 μmol/kg / 89.71%; eucalyptus leaves 762.56 μmol/kg / 76.15%; mussel shell 501.46 μmol/kg / 48.15%; pine bark 294.23 μmol/kg / 29.38%. These are observed loadings under one tested condition, not fitted qmax values.
Model / metric: Observed table loading and percentage removal at highest measured C0
Evidence status: Extracted from supplied main PDF; SI not supplied
Caveat / follow-up: Do not relabel observed loadings as qmax. Pine-bark removal is non-monotonic: 38.73% at measured C0 = 38.62 μmol/L versus 29.38% at 52.07 μmol/L. Preserve this source result rather than smoothing the trend.

Adsorbent / material: Ground eucalyptus leaves, pine bark, pine needles, wood ash and mussel shell by-products
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — raw/minimally processed biomass and by-product biosorbents
Evidence domain: Model validity, sorbent chemistry and desorption
Experimental design / conditions: Authors fitted Freundlich, Langmuir and linear/partition-coefficient models. Results table indicates high fit errors or no valid fit for some sorbents; discussion says Langmuir fitting is invalid because of high errors. Desorption test was carried out after adsorption at the maximum AMX concentration.
Reported result: No release was detected in the reported desorption procedure. The authors identify pine needles, eucalyptus leaves and wood ash as stronger AMX-retaining materials; model fits were material-specific and did not support a single reliable fitted-capacity ranking across all five.
Value / units: No release detected in the reported desorption test; no validated qmax common to all five sorbents
Model / metric: Authors’ model-fit assessment and batch desorption result
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 4, Table 2 and discussion; PDF p. 5, §4 Conclusions
Evidence status: Extracted from supplied main PDF; SI not supplied
Caveat / follow-up: The main text reports mussel-shell pH as 9.39 in one passage and 9.04 elsewhere; cited supplementary Table S1 was not supplied. Langmuir is explicitly described as invalid for the data because of high error. Do not force one qmax comparison.
